newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl allies worry tax reform plan falls short.
newsitem.headline: Kohl allies worry tax reform plan falls short.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's planned tax reform, meant as the centrepiece of his 1998 reelection drive, has provoked deep concern among his own supporters that it will be too little, too late to please German voters.

Bold tax cut proposals, to be unveiled on Thursday, were conceived as a popular step similar to -- although not as radical as -- the supply-side policies the United States and Britain introduced in the 1980s.
But weeks of political wrangling, soured by parallel talk of raising VAT and other taxes to recoup lost revenues, appear to have watered down the good news Bonn wanted to announce.

Several younger leaders in Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), fearing a mini-reform will weaken their chances in state elections, have gone so far as to call for Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign.
The criticism has not hit Kohl yet, but the frequent talk about the general election almost two years away shows how much CDU politicians see riding on the reform Waigel produces.
"This tax reform will be decisive for the election," Guenther Oettinger, the CDU leader in the Baden-Wuerttemberg state assembly, declared on Tuesday.

"We need to change tax laws to boost investment and create jobs. If voters see that visible changes are coming, we'll win the general election. If the whole thing remains cloudy and ends in a dispute, we'll be significantly weakened."

Kohl's centre-right coalition, now in its record 14th year in office, is weak enough already. The latest Emnid poll showed it running at 43 percent support compared to 48 percent for the opposition Social Democrats and Greens together.
The chancellor's majority has shrunk with each of the four elections he has won and he now has only 12 votes more than the opposition in a parliament of 672 deputies.

The reform is expected to drop the top income tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent now. Among the unpopular suggestions to help make up for the lost revenues are a VAT increase -- one or two percentage points is a matter of dispute -- and new taxes on some pensions and life insurance policies.

Waigel also wants to close the tax code's many loopholes but lobbies are fighting back. His own Christian Social Union (CSU) party, afraid of losing its majority at Bavaria's next state election, is baulking at cutting breaks for commuters because so many rural voters there have long drives to work.
Herbert Hax, chairman of Kohl's panel of economic advisors, said on Wednesday the wrangling had already turned many businessmen off considering new investment in Germany.

"The positive effect that the announcement of a tax reform could have had has already been debated away," he told the Berliner Morgenpost daily. "A businessman in Germany doesn't know these days how things will develop."

A new twist to this tax debate is that up-and-coming CDU leaders in the states have kept up their criticism despite the gruff rebuff Kohl gave them. One broadside from the veteran chancellor is usually enough to restore peace in the ranks.

But these local leaders have their own power bases and a sharp ear for grass roots discontent. Kohl also needs them to fight important state polls in 1998 and 1999 if he wants to overturn the SPD's majority in the upper house of parliament.
So younger politicians like Christian Wulff, the CDU's Lower Saxony state leader, have brushed off Kohl's remarks and kept calling for a real reform instead of cosmetic changes.
Ole von Beust, CDU leader in the city-state of Hamburg, said: "I fear the CDU is not seen as the tax-cutting party but the party of tax increases. That will be devastating for us."
Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung said the younger leaders were clearly concerned Kohl's towering image might not be enough to bring home victory at the next election.
"The younger CDU politicians in parliament and in the states are thinking of the post-Kohl era and do not want to be blamed then for opportunities missed today," it wrote.
